person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: parents as five named positions on vaccination - A CONTROLLED VOCABULARY BUILT BY CROSSWALKING THREE INCOMPATIBLE TAXONOMIES, with a prevalence attached to each category
span.quote: Five distinct parental groups were identified: the ‘unquestioning acceptor’ (30–40%), the ‘cautious acceptor’ (25–35%); the ‘hesitant’ (20–30%); the ‘late or selective vaccinator’ (2–27%); and the

span.label: how a health professional should talk to a parent about vaccination, given that what to say depends on which kind of parent they are
span.quote: We found nine papers advising health professionals on communicating with patients about vaccination but none that tailored communication to empirically derived parental positions

span.label: five parental positions with prevalence ranges, each mapped to prior classifications and to a stage of the Transtheoretical Model, with tailored communication goals and strategies
span.quote: The parental positions described in this paper act as a starting point for health professionals to choose the most appropriate communication strategy. Naturally these will vary according to the parent

span.label: method
span.quote: We reviewed the classifications presented within the three identified studies, [ 28 - 30 ] summarised parental positions from each study, and discussed their relevance to vaccine communication. A discrete number of parental positions relating to vaccination attitudes and behaviour were proposed, discussed and revised based on the categories’ applicability to clinical interactions and international relevance. The final set of five parental positions are described in Table 2 . A range for the approximate proportion of each group is given based on population surveys or registers from the USA, European Union, New Zealand, and Australia

span.label: parental vaccine attitudes distributed across a spectrum that no single prior study had described exhaustively
span.quote: The literature review informing the parental positions found only three papers providing a spectrum of attitudes to vaccination.

span.label: systematic search of four databases (3,168 hits to 112 to 3 usable studies), reconciliation of the three classifications into five positions, prevalence ranges from population surveys in four regions, and a face-validity survey of 104 nurses
span.term: systematic search of four databases (3,168 hits to 112 to 3 usable studies), reconciliation of the three classifications into five positions, prevalence ranges from population surveys in four regions, and a face-validity survey of 104 nurses
span.quote: The searches identified 3168 total hits (including duplicates) which was reduced to 112 after screening titles and removing duplicates. Of these, we identified three studies that proposed a spectrum spanning the parental positions on vaccination.

span.label: THE VOCABULARY IS A CROSSWALK, AND THE PAPER SHOWS ITS WORKING. Three prior studies with three incompatible category sets - Gust's five attitudinal clusters, Downs's two decision-making types, Benin's vaccinator/non-vaccinator tree - reconciled into five positions, with each mapping stated: `In Gust's study, they CORRESPONDED WITH the immunisation advocates or go along to get along groups`; `Both this category and unquestioning acceptors were DRAWN FROM Benin's category of vaccination acceptors`; `they MOST CLOSELY CORRESPOND TO the fence-sitter`
span.quote: These parents vaccinate, or want to, vaccinate their children and have no specific questions about the safety and necessity of vaccines. In Gust’s study, they corresponded with the ‘immunisation advocates’ or ‘go along to get along’ groups who see the importance of childhood vaccination and are confident in its safety

span.label: AND A SECOND CROSSWALK ONTO A THEORY OF BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: `The majority of parents are in the ACTION AND MAINTENANCE stage (cautious or unquestioning acceptors). Some will be CONTEMPLATING or even PREPARING to immunise - WHAT WE DESCRIBE AS HESITANT parents ... Vaccine refusers are usually in the PRE-CONTEMPLATION stage`. The five positions are simultaneously an attitude taxonomy and a stage model
span.quote: The majority of parents are in the action and maintenance stage (cautious or unquestioning acceptors). Some will be contemplating or even preparing to immunise – what we describe as ‘hesitant’ parents. Late or selective vaccinators, who are willing to have some vaccines, may also contemplate full vaccination if guided by a health professional [ 5 ]. ‘Vaccine refusers’ are usually in the pre-contemplation stage where they are not considering vaccinating at all.

span.label: the design criterion for the vocabulary is EXHAUSTIVENESS, and it is printed: `we sought to identify only studies that would provide a spectrum of attitudinal positions that would THEORETICALLY ACCOUNT FOR ALL PARENTS`. Three of 112 screened papers met it
span.quote: While there is a vast literature exploring attitudes to vaccination among parents [ 3 , 7 , 74 , 75 ], we sought to identify only studies that would provide a spectrum of attitudinal positions that would theoretically account for all parents.

span.label: and the failure mode it is designed against is the INFORMATION DEFICIT MODEL: poor communication `often results from A BELIEF BY THE HEALTH PROFESSIONAL THAT VACCINE REFUSAL ARISES FROM IGNORANCE which can simply be addressed by persuading or providing more information ... and MAY EVEN RESULT IN A BACKFIRE EFFECT`
span.quote: Such poor communication often results from a belief by the health professional that vaccine refusal arises from ignorance which can simply be addressed by persuading or providing more information. Such an approach is counter-productive because it fails to account for the complexity of reasons underpinning vaccine refusal and may even result in a backfire effect

span.label: THE CATEGORIES ARE NOT STABLE AND THE PAPER SAYS SO: `the spectrum described DOES SIMPLIFY what is often a complex process of decision making WHICH MAY INVOLVE PARENTS MOVING BETWEEN POSITIONS OVER TIME`. A discrete five-way classification of something the authors describe as continuous and time-varying - the same tension macdonald2015 states about hesitancy, arriving here from the practice end three years earlier
span.quote: However, the spectrum described does simplify what is often a complex process of decision making which may involve parents moving between positions over time.

span.label: THE VOCABULARY RESTS ON THREE US STUDIES TOTALLING 647 PEOPLE, two of them n=30 and n=33: `While the parental positions were developed from THREE US STUDIES, we have applied our knowledge and experience from other countries to their modification`, and the proportions `WILL VARY OVER TIME, WITHIN REGIONS, AND BETWEEN PRACTICES`
span.quote: While the parental positions were developed from three US studies, we have applied our knowledge and experience from other countries to their modification. The approximate proportions of each parental group are estimates from population-based surveys and will vary over time, within regions, and between practices.

span.label: one category's extension is uncertain by a factor of THIRTEEN - `late or selective vaccinator` is given as 2-27% - and the smallest category fails exactly where it matters: `the estimate for the percentage of parents completely refusing all vaccines is given as LESS THAN 2% based on population data BUT THERE ARE CLUSTERS OF MUCH HIGHER REFUSER RATES IN SPECIFIC LOCALITIES`
span.quote: For example, the estimate for the percentage of parents completely refusing all vaccines is given as less than 2% based on population data but there are clusters of much higher refuser rates in specific localities [ 43 , 44 , 77 ]. Nevertheless, giving ranges for the sizes of the groups may assist health professionals and programme coordinators in planning for targeted information and strategies.

span.label: the framework has FACE VALIDITY AND NOTHING ELSE, which the paper states plainly: 104 nurses gave a median usefulness of 8.8 and `74% rated the framework as VERY REALISTIC`, but `Communication strategies to date have LACKED CLEAR EVIDENCE OF EFFICACY in vaccination settings ... now needs to be MORE FULLY EVALUATED` by a randomised trial that had not been done
span.quote: Communication strategies to date have lacked clear evidence of efficacy in vaccination settings. We have described a framework for talking with parents about vaccination. It is informed by evidence and acceptable to the health professionals involved in the formative evaluation sessions, but now needs to be more fully evaluated. This may involve group or individual training of health professionals who undergo assessment using standardised patients and validated scales that measure quality of communication [ 78 ]. To measure effectiveness of the framework against the aims described above (satisfaction, self-efficacy, decision quality and vaccination uptake), a randomised controlled trial delivered at cluster (e.g., GP practice) or individual level would then establish its effectiveness compared with

span.label: a face-validity survey of 104 accredited nurse immunisation providers, plus verbal feedback from 20 coordinators, experts and a consumer representative
span.note: eliminates: the objection that a framework built from three US studies would be unrecognisable in practice - `74% rated the framework as VERY REALISTIC, 26% as SOMEWHAT REALISTIC, while NO-ONE rated it as not at all realistic` · outcome: held
span.quote: To assess general acceptability of the framework and recommendations, accredited nurse immunisation providers were presented with them in three annual update sessions, and 104 completed a short questionnaire about usefulness (scored from 1 ‘not at all useful’ to 10 ‘extremely useful’), realism (not at all/somewhat/very), strengths (open question), and areas for improvement (open question). Feedback was positive with a median score for usefulness of 8.8 (range 3–10); 74% rated the framework as ‘very realistic’, 26% as ‘somewhat realistic’, while no-one rated it as

span.note: eliminates: the objection that the five positions were chosen rather than found; the criterion was stated in advance - a spectrum that would `THEORETICALLY ACCOUNT FOR ALL PARENTS` - and only three papers met it · outcome: partial
span.quote: The searches identified 3168 total hits (including duplicates) which was reduced to 112 after screening titles and removing duplicates. Of these, we identified three studies that proposed a spectrum spanning the parental positions on vaccination.

span.note: eliminates: nothing, and the paper names the trial that would do it: `a randomised controlled trial delivered at cluster ... or individual level WOULD THEN ESTABLISH ITS EFFECTIVENESS compared with usual care` · outcome: absent-declared-unreported

span.label: immunisation advocates
span.quote: These parents vaccinate, or want to, vaccinate their children and have no specific questions about the safety and necessity of vaccines. In Gust’s study, they corresponded with the ‘immunisation advocates’ or ‘go along to get along’ groups who see the importance of childhood vaccination and are confident in its safety

span.label: fence-sitter
span.quote: The hesitant 20–30% These parents vaccinate their child but have significant concerns [ 29 ]. In Gust’s study, they most closely correspond to the ‘fence-sitter’ who only slightly agrees about the benefits and safety of vaccination and is neutral about their relationship and trust with their healthcare provider

span.label: vaccination acceptors
span.quote: These parents vaccinate their children despite minor concerns. They may exhibit a ‘hope and pray’ mentality recognising that vaccines carry rare but serious side effects and hoping that their child is not affected [ 45 ]. Both this category and ‘unquestioning acceptors’ were drawn from Benin’s category of ‘vaccination acceptors’

span.label: Transtheoretical Model
span.quote: It should also be borne in mind that motivational interviewing builds upon the Transtheoretical Model [ 68 ]. This is a framework for understanding the process of behaviour change where individuals may pass through five stages: precontemplation , where they are not considering change; contemplation , where they seriously consider change; preparation , where they plan and commit to change; action , where they make a specific behavioural change which if successful, leads to maintenance of that behaviour, the fifth stage.

span.label: framework
span.quote: It should also be borne in mind that motivational interviewing builds upon the Transtheoretical Model [ 68 ]. This is a framework for understanding the process of behaviour change where individuals may pass through five stages: precontemplation , where they are not considering change; contemplation , where they seriously consider change; preparation , where they plan and commit to change; action , where they make a specific behavioural change which if successful, leads to maintenance of that behaviour, the fifth stage.

span.label: guiding style
span.quote: Evidence from other areas of healthcare practice suggests adapting the principles of motivational interviewing. This is a form of communication that uses a guiding style, rather than a directing style, for discussions where there is ambivalence and resistance to change

span.label: directing style

Such an approach is counter-productive because it fails to account for the complexity of reasons underpinning vaccine refusal and may even result in a backfire effect

span.label: `the hesitant` HERE - ONE OF FIVE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE POSITIONS, at 20-30%, defined behaviourally as parents who `VACCINATE THEIR CHILD BUT HAVE SIGNIFICANT CONCERNS` and mapped to Gust's `fence-sitter`. A BIN, not a scale
span.quote: The hesitant 20–30% These parents vaccinate their child but have significant concerns [ 29 ]. In Gust’s study, they most closely correspond to the ‘fence-sitter’ who only slightly agrees about the benefits and safety of vaccination and is neutral about their relationship and trust with their healthcare provider

span.label: `late or selective vaccinator` - THE ONLY POSITION DEFINED BY WHAT THE PARENT DOES RATHER THAN BELIEVES: `Concerns about vaccination result in this group CHOOSING TO DELAY OR SELECT ONLY SOME recommended vaccines`. And it is porous - `With a specific vaccine scare hesitant parents may SELECT-OUT the vaccine and MOVE TO THIS CATEGORY`
span.quote: Late or selective vaccinator 2–27% Concerns about vaccination result in this group choosing to delay or select only some recommended vaccines [ 38 ]. This group most closely correspond with Gust’s ‘worried’ category with significant doubts about the safety and some doubt about the necessity of vaccines

span.label: `unquestioning acceptor` - A CATEGORY BUILT BY MERGING TWO OF GUST'S: `In Gust's study, they CORRESPONDED WITH the immunisation advocates OR go along to get along groups`. Two source categories, one target, and the merge is stated but not justified
span.quote: These parents vaccinate, or want to, vaccinate their children and have no specific questions about the safety and necessity of vaccines.
